webpage.text:
M83’s New Song Is the Sonic Equivalent of ‘Space Junk’ — Which Is Also What Their New Album Is About

Didn’t see this coming. Photo: Jon Kopaloff/Getty Images

What do you get when you set out to make an album inspired by Who’s the Boss? and Punky Brewster? Space garbage, it seems — or so “Do It, Try It,” off M83’s first album since 2011’s Hurry Up, We’re Dreaming (remember “Midnight City“?), would suggest. It’s a mishmash of goofy synths and keys that perhaps our present selves are not yet equipped to appreciate. After all, as Anthony Gonzalez explains, both the song and the album Junk (out April 8) are just a meditation on the meaningless of human existence: “Anything we create today is going to end up being space junk at one point anyway, and I find it really fascinating and scary at the same time — beautiful too in a way. I have this image of pieces of humanity floating in space, lost forever.” Gonzalez has also said this will be a more “eclectic” showing from M83, which means the album features Beck and Susanne Sundfør; nothing says eclectic like Beck. Meet the sound of M83’s new tomorrow.

webpage.text:
M83's 'You and the Night' disappoints | Life

Two out of five stars 

After M83’s popular single release, “Midnight City” in 2011, the band has the public expecting the best from pop-synth genius Anthony Gonzalez. However, what happened was the quite opposite.

Their newest album, “You and the Night,” is a soundtrack to the scandalous French film, “Meetings After Midnight.” Gonzalez, the mastermind behind M83, worked in collaboration with his brother Yann Gonzalez, the director and writer of the film, to create what sounds like one song on repeat.

M83 announced before the release of the album that it isn’t for listeners who only like “Midnight City.”

We were warned, and yet we still listened to track after track of nothing but piano, violins and other orchestral instruments. 

The first track, “L’inconnu,” meaning “unknown” or “stranger,” starts off with sounds of waves crashing, similar to something from “Pirates of the Caribbean.” With the scent of sea salt fresh in our nostrils, the next song, “Nous,” includes high, breathy vocals — making us wonder if we are listening to Ariel from “The Little Mermaid.”

With mellow romantic undertones and few vocals, the listener is transported to a fantasy land. It’s the perfect album to listen to during a UREC yoga class, or when taking a quick power nap. However, with this soundtrack playing you might not wake up from Shavasana yoga or make it to your test.

Keep in mind that this is a soundtrack; it has fewer spoken words than Disney/Pixar’s “WALL-E.”

Track four on the album, “A La Lumière Des Diamants,” sounds similar to something from “Titanic.” Melodies hypnotize the listener, with hallucinations of a young Kate Winslet and Leonardo DiCaprio frolicking around a cruise ship. Unfortunately, this song is far less impressive than “My Heart Will Go On.”

The only non-drowsy song off the entire soundtrack is the last track, “Un Nouveau Soleil,” offering listeners a chance to wake themselves up. The uncharacteristically cheery final tune could be off of any soundtrack whether it’s “Pocahontas” or any final goodbye scenes.

Although bland at times, the album flows well as a whole.

The most exciting part of this album is the plot of the film it is written for: “Meetings After Midnight,” which is translated from its original French title, “Les Rencontres d’apres Minuit.”

The film the soundtrack is based on has an erotic yet familiar feel to it.

According to IMDb, “Meetings After Midnight” is about “a young couple and their transvestite maid preparing for an orgy. The guests will be the slut, the star, the stud and the teen.” At the Cannes film festival, viewers compared it to a dirty version of “The Breakfast Club.”

The scandalous film steals the spotlight, but it is undetermined whether the soundtrack truly makes the movie, or if it is just an afterthought.

In the future, I hope to see less soundtracks from M83, and more focus on their original creative genius. No one can complain about a repeat of “Hurry Up, We’re Dreaming,” but seriously M83, this soundtrack has us thinking, “'Hurry Up, We’re Dreaming' of a better album!"

Dominique Lategano is a sophomore media arts and design major. Contact her at lategada@dukes.jmu.edu.
